 Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride can stake a claim as one of the NFL’s best

 INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 18: Trey McBride #85 of the Arizona Cardinals catches a pass against Quentin Lake #37 of the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) 
 By Parker Gabriel | pgabriel@denverpost.com | The Denver Post PUBLISHED: October 24, 2026 at 6:00 AM MDT | UPDATED: October 24, 2026 at 4:12 PM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... When the Broncos defense takes the field for the first time Sunday against Arizona, priority No. 1 will be clear.
 Slow down the kid from Fort Morgan.
 That, of course, is Cardinals tight end Trey McBride, the one-man wrecking crew who can stake his claim at 26 years old as the best all-around tight end in the NFL.
 Through six games this season, McBride is tied with reigning offensive player of the year and WR Seattle Jaxon Smith-Njigba atop the heap of pass-catchers with 49 catches. It’s more than just volume, though.
 A tight end like McBride allows you to play the personnel groupings you want to play. Move him around. Force a defense into deciding if it wants to treat him like he’s part of a run-heavy package or treat him more like a wide receiver.
 He is, to use a term that’s become kind of a running joke around Denver, a joker.
 “It’s (Los Angeles) Rams similarities with the 13 personnel, so he can get big on you, but that big can go small with the pass game with McBride,” defensive coordinator Vance Joseph said this week.
 Head coach Sean Payton likened McBride to another terrific tight end the Broncos see twice a year in Las Vegas, Brock Bowers, saying, “These are unique skill set tight ends that can get matched up on safeties or even corners.
 “He has really good feel, really good transition, and they’re doing a really good job of moving him around.”
 There is a bit of irony in the fact that McBride is a Colorado kid and a former Colorado State standout who went No. 55 overall in the 2022 draft. Denver didn’t have a first-rounder that year after the Russell Wilson trade and eventually took an All-Pro of their own nine picks later in outside linebacker Nik Bonitto.
 Bonitto is a perfect example of the way the Broncos have built to their current status as one of the more talented and stable rosters in football. They’ve found premium talent in all corners of the draft, via free agency and by trade. They’ve developed players more than they’ve imported, and they’ve done it well.
What they have not done is find a player anywhere near McBride at tight end.
 Perhaps it’s fitting that the Broncos and Cardinals are playing on National Tight Ends Day.
 Denver gets reliable play out of Adam Trautman and Nate Adkins —Payton puts a premium on players from whom he knows exactly what to expect — and he has a lottery ticket in development in Caleb Lohner. They hoped to get a dynamic pass-catcher in Evan Engram last spring, and he’s made some big plays, but he’s not the kind of true matchup weapon that the top-tier tight ends are at this stage in his career.
 Every time a McBride, a Bowers, a George Kittle or Travis Kelce lines up against Denver, it’s a reminder of the value of that position and of the Broncos’ inability to identify one over the past decade.
 McBride this year has 361 yards and a trio of touchdown catches to go with his 49 grabs. The Broncos tight ends in total have 18 catches for 180 yards and three touchdowns.
 McBride last year caught 126 passes for 1,239 yards and 11 touchdowns. That is 48 more catches, 520 more yards and eight more touchdowns than Denver’s group produced, despite it being the best season for Broncos tight ends of the Payton era so far.
 It’s not always an easy position group to evaluate. Bowers jumped clean off the screen and only fell to No. 13 in the 2024 draft because six quarterbacks, including Denver’s Bo Nix, went in the first 12 picks. Budding stars like Chicago’s Colston Loveland and Indianapolis’ Tyler Warren went in the first round, too, much to the chagrin of the Broncos, who watched them come off the board at Nos. 10 and 14, respectively, while they held the No. 20 pick in 2025. McBride, though, was picked in the middle of the second round. Kittle and Kelce were middle-rounders, as was Green Bay’s Tucker Kraft.
 More and more, though, the best tight ends get picked early. So part of the question, longer term, is where the Broncos are going to find their own version of McBride, even if it’s McBride Lite.
 He’s the style of player Payton made a killing with in New Orleans over several different options, including Jeremy Shockey, Jimmy Graham and Ben Watson.
 He’s the style of player who could actually help unlock another level for the Denver offense.

 Tight ends like this, similar to any other position, don’t come available all that often. If the Broncos don’t think they’re likely to find one in the draft, it’s at least worth poking around to see if there’s any room for a deal around the trade deadline.
 Just this week, Detroit’s Sam LaPorta went on a podcast and griped about the lack of a contract extension before this fall, the final year of his rookie deal. Payton knows Lions coach Dan Campbell — himself a former Payton tight end — as well as any other coach in the league. Is it likely? Probably not. The Lions might be able to stay in the mix and they don’t have much incentive to deal a reliably upper-echelon player, but it’s worth a check, and it’s worth real draft capital.
 Otherwise, the search will likely continue for a while. The Broncos have established players at so many positions, and the framework of the future is in place at many, too.
 Tight end has been perhaps the most difficult to solve on both fronts.
